title: A Phase 2b, randomised, open-label study to characterize the immune response to vaccination and revaccination dose with non-adjuvanted and adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine in young and older adults
official: A Phase 2b, randomised, open-label study to characterize the immune response to vaccination and revaccination dose with non-adjuvanted and adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine in young and older adults
summary:
Background and study aims
This study aims to better understand how people’s immune systems respond to a vaccine designed to protect against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a common virus that can cause serious illness, particularly in older adults. Although RSV vaccines are now available, there is still limited information on how long protection lasts, how the immune response differs by age, and whether repeat (booster) doses can improve or sustain immunity over time.

Who can participate?
The study will include healthy younger adults (aged 18–45 years) and older adults (aged 68–72 years).

What does the study involve?
 Participants will receive two doses of an RSV vaccine, which targets a key part of the virus that helps the immune system recognise and fight infection. The study compares two versions of the vaccine: one with an adjuvant (a substance that enhances the immune responses) and one without. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of these groups.
Over the course of three years, researchers will collect blood samples at several time points to measure how strong and long-lasting the immune response is after vaccination and revaccination. In addition, some participants will take part in more detailed studies of immune responses at the site where infections occur. These may include fine needle aspirates (FNAs), which involve taking a small sample of cells from lymph nodes, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), a procedure that collects samples from the lungs using a small amount of fluid. These procedures help researchers understand how the immune system works locally in tissues, not just in the bloodstream.
By comparing responses between younger and older adults, and between  two vaccine types, the study will provide important information on how best to optimise RSV vaccination. It will help determine whether adding an adjuvant improves protection, whether booster doses are beneficial, and how immunity changes over time.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Benefits:
Not provided at time of registration
Risks:
Vaccine:
Intra-muscular vaccination commonly causes a transient and self-limiting local inflammatory reaction. This may
typically include discomfort, redness and swelling, and some volunteers may feel generally unwell in themselves for a short time.
Anaphylaxis is a rare but a potentially life-threatening allergic reaction and may occur (very rarely) after immunisation.
All clinical staff are trained in the immediate treatment of anaphylactic reactions including the use of intra-muscular
adrenaline.

Blood sampling:
This may cause slight pain and sometimes bruising. Occasionally, people feel light-headed, nauseous (feeling sick), or faint. The amount of blood taken at each visit is small and should not cause any problems to healthy adults.

Fine needle aspiration:
This can be painful and therefore local anaesthetic is used to numb the area. As with any minor medical procedure the risks include bleeding, bruising, infection, swelling and tenderness. An ultrasound is used to mitigate the risk to surrounding structures by guiding the needle. In a study previously lead by the chief investigator, all adverse events related to FNA were mild and self limiting.

Bronchoscopy and nasal sampling:
Possible bronchoscopy risks and symptoms include more common side effects such as mild discomfort, cough and sore nose/throat and hoarseness and much rarer side effects such as bleeding, pneumothorax, aspiration pneumoniae, fever, arrythmia, disorientation, agitation and cardiorespiratory depression. These side effects are minimised by offering appropriate analgesia and sedation, asking participants to be nil by mouth, and specific bronchoscopy techniques and procedures for example.
Possible nasal biopsy risks include mild nasal discomfort or rhinorrhoea following the procedure, which typically settles within 48 hours. Rarely, participants may have an adverse reaction to the local anaesthetic used. The risk of local bleeding which may require further outpatient ENT intervention such as nasal packing or cautery is <1%. Rarely, participants may need to be admitted for observation to an ENT acute ward for management of bleeding. Surgical intervention to manage epistaxis in the operating theatre following this procedure is extremely rare. The study is designed to ensure any risk is minimal by appropriate study team expertise, design, careful participant selection and rigours safety procedures. Participants will be provided with information regarding these expected adverse events in the participant information sheet and adverse events will be monitored and reported. Participants will be observed for a period of time following these procedures.

Where is the study run from?
Oxford Vaccine Group (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
December 2026 to April 2030.

Who is funding the study?
GlaxoSmithKline (UK).

Who is the main contact?
Simon.Drysdale@paediatrics.ox.ac.uk

interventions.name: Non-adjuvanted RSV PreF3 [RSV PreF3 Vaccine] , Arexvy [RSVPreF3 antigen, AS01E Adjuvant System]

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Participants who, in the opinion of the investigator, can and will comply with the requirements of the protocol (e.g., attend study site visits, ability to access and utilize a phone or other electronic communications)
2. Written or witnessed informed consent obtained from the participant prior to performance of any study-specific procedure
3. Participants who are medically stable in the opinion of the investigator at study entry. Participants with chronic stable medical conditions with or without specific treatment, such as diabetes, hypertension or cardiac disease, are allowed to participate in this study, if considered by the investigator as medically stable. A stable medical condition is defined as disease not requiring significant change in therapy or hospitalization for worsening disease during 3 months before enrolment
4. Male or female participant age 18 to 45 years at the time of the first RSV vaccination with the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine or non-adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine
5. Male or female participant age 68 to 72 years at the time of the first RSV vaccination with the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine or non-adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine
6. Participants of childbearing* potential may be enrolled in the study, if the participant: 
has practiced adequate contraception from 1 month prior to study intervention administration, and has a negative pregnancy test on the day of study prior to intervention administration**, and has agreed to continue adequate contraception for at least 1 month after completion of the study intervention administration. (refer to contraception guidance) 
*Participants in the following categories are considered participants of childbearing potential (POCBP (fertile)) if:  
Adolescents of childbearing potential: Tanner stage ≥2 (post-thelarche) irrespective of the occurrence of menarche or following menarche. 
From the time of menarche until becoming postmenopausal unless permanently sterile. 
Note: Menarche is the first onset of menses in a young female. Menarche is normally preceded by several changes associated with puberty including breast development and pubic hair growth. 
**A urine pregnancy test must be performed for all participants of childbearing potential before the administration of the first dose of study intervention. Pregnancy testing must be done even if the participant is menstruating at the time of the study visit. The study intervention may only be administered if the pregnancy test is negative.
Exclusion criteria:
1.	History of any reaction or hypersensitivity likely to be exacerbated by any component of the study intervention(s)
2.	Any confirmed or suspected immunosuppressive or immunodeficient condition, based on medical history and physical examination (no laboratory testing required)
3.	Chronic respiratory disease, e.g.: 
3.1. Poorly controlled asthma 
3.2. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) 
3.3. Bronchiectasis 
3.4. Cystic fibrosis 
3.5. Interstitial lung fibrosis 
3.6. Pneumoconiosis 
3.7. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
4.	Hypersensitivity to latex
5.	Acute or unstable chronic conditions, as determined by physical examination and/or laboratory screening tests
6.	Recurrent history or uncontrolled neurological disorders or any neuroinflammatory condition, including, but not limited to: 
6.1. Demyelinating disorders 
6.2. Encephalitis or myelitis of any origin 
6.3. Congenital neurological conditions 
6.4. Encephalopathies 
6.5. Seizures, including all subtypes such as: 
6.5.1. Absence seizures 
6.5.2. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures 
6.5.3. Partial complex seizures 
6.5.4. Partial simple seizures
7.	Any other clinical condition that, in the opinion of the investigator, might put the participant or their contacts at risk because of participation in the study, adversely affect the interpretation of the study results, or impair the participant’s ability to participate in the study
8.	Participants who are pregnant, lactating, or intending on becoming pregnant during the study
9.	Any condition that, in the judgment of the investigator, would make intramuscular injection unsafe
10.	Significant underlying illness that, in the opinion of the investigator, would be expected to prevent completion of the study
11.	Any history of dementia or any medical condition that moderately or severely impairs cognition and understanding of the informed consent form and/or study procedures
12.	HIV infection
13.	Hepatitis B or C infection
14.	Prior RSV immunisation through administration of any RSV vaccine or RSV monoclonal antibody up to 5 years prior to enrolment
15.	Use of any investigational or non-registered product (drug, vaccine or invasive medical device in the country of enrolment) other than the study intervention(s) during the period beginning 30 days before the first dose of study intervention(s) (Day -29 to Day 1), or planned use during the study period
16.	Administration of immunoglobulins or other blood products or plasma derivatives during the period starting 90 days before the study intervention, or planned administration during the study period
17.	Chronic administration of immune-modifying drugs (defined as more than 14 consecutive days in total) and/or planned use of long-acting immune-modifying treatments at any time up to the end of the study: 
17.1. Up to 90 days prior to the study intervention administration: for corticosteroids, this will mean prednisone equivalent ≥20 mg/day for adult participants. Inhaled, intra-articular/intra-bursal and topical steroids are allowed for enrolment in the study; however, bronchoscopy-specific exclusion criteria apply for use of corticosteroids 
17.2. Up to 6 months prior to study intervention administration: long-acting immune-modifying drugs, including, among others, immunotherapy (e.g., TNF inhibitors), monoclonal antibodies and antitumoral medication
18.	Planned administration/administration of a vaccine in the period starting 30 days before the dose and ending 14 days after the dose of study intervention administration, or within 14 days prior to any subsequent blood sampling timepoints
19.	Concurrent clinical study experience
20.	History of/current chronic alcohol consumption and/or drug abuse, based on the investigator’s judgment
21.	Any study personnel or their immediate dependents, family or household members
22.	Bedridden participants
